notions.titre: Television and the Unique Selling Proposition
notions.question: How did television transform American advertising in the 1950s?
notions.definition: Television spread very rapidly through American households: fewer than 10% owned a set in 1950, nearly 90% in 1960. It became the leading medium of postwar mass consumption. At first, a single advertiser sponsored an entire program, which often bore its name (sponsorship); after the quiz show scandals (1958-1959), the networks took back control of programming and sold commercial slots to several advertisers (spots). Rosser Reeves, of the Ted Bates agency, formalized the "Unique Selling Proposition" (USP) in "Reality in Advertising" (1961): each ad must make a specific proposition, one that the competition does not make, and one strong enough to attract new customers, repeated relentlessly (example: M&M's, "melts in your mouth, not in your hand"). In 1952 Reeves also created the "Eisenhower Answers America" spots, marking the entry of television advertising into presidential campaigns.

items: Proposition: a concrete benefit for the consumer
Unique: the competition does not (or cannot) put it forward
Strong: able to make people switch brands
Repetition: the same message, over a long period, at high frequency

lignes: One advertiser finances and controls a program
The network sells slots to several advertisers

termes.definition: Financing of a program by an advertiser.
Time slot with the largest audience.

exemple.texte: Rosser Reeves's slogan for M&M's, "melts in your mouth, not in your hand," illustrates the USP: a concrete benefit, specific to the product, repeated for years.

confusions.explication: The USP must state a distinctive benefit, not just a catchy phrase.

verification: What are Reeves's three conditions for a USP?

notions.question: What was the "creative revolution," and how did it break with the advertising of the 1950s?
notions.definition: In the 1960s, a new generation of New York advertising people rejected the hammering repetition of the USP and what they saw as the condescending advertising of the 1950s. Bill Bernbach (Doyle Dane Bernbach agency, DDB, founded in 1949) had copywriters and art directors work together, and relied on humor, apparent honesty and the reader's intelligence. His campaign for Volkswagen ("Think Small," 1959) presented a small German car as a smart choice compared with big American cars; his campaign for Avis ("We try harder," 1962) turned second place into a selling point. David Ogilvy (Ogilvy & Mather) combined elegance, research and brand image (the Hathaway man with the eye patch, 1951; Rolls-Royce, 1958); Leo Burnett, in Chicago, created iconic characters (the Marlboro Man, 1955). According to the historian Thomas Frank, this creative revolution co-opted the codes of the counterculture (nonconformism, irony) in order to sell: "hip consumerism."

termes.definition: Pair made up of a copywriter and an art director.
Making fun of oneself, here of one's own product.
How the brand is represented in the public's mind.

exemple.texte: DDB's "Think Small" ad for the Volkswagen Beetle (1959) shows a tiny car in a large white space with ironic copy: it became the emblem of the creative revolution.

confusions.explication: According to Frank, advertising appropriated the codes of the counterculture rather than being part of it.

verification: Why is "Think Small" a reversal of the car ads of the time?

choix.explication: A figure of the creative revolution.

choix.texte: The rigged quiz show scandals discredited advertisers' control of programs
choix.explication: The networks regained control of programming.

questions.enonce: Which characteristics belong to the creative revolution?

choix.texte: Hammering repetition of a single argument
Co-opting the codes of the counterculture

questions.enonce: What does Thomas Frank mean by "hip consumerism"?

choix.texte: Consumption presented as nonconformist and rebellious
choix.explication: Advertising sells rebellion as a lifestyle.

flashcards.question: Explain the rise of television advertising and the USP.
flashcards.reponse: Household ownership: < 10% in 1950, ≈ 90% in 1960. Program sponsorship, then spots after the quiz show scandals (1958-1959). USP (Reeves, Ted Bates, 1961): a concrete, unique proposition, strong enough to make people switch brands, repeated (M&M's). "Eisenhower Answers America" spots (1952).

flashcards.question: What was the creative revolution?
flashcards.reponse: 1960s: rejection of repetition and of a condescending tone. Bernbach (DDB): copywriter + art director team, humor, apparent honesty (VW "Think Small" 1959, Avis "We try harder" 1962). Ogilvy: brand image (Hathaway, Rolls-Royce). Burnett: the Marlboro Man. Thomas Frank: co-opting of the counterculture, "hip consumerism."
flashcards.relance: How does Avis turn a weakness into a selling point?
